Before sunrise, the city belongs to people who unlock doors. A baker shakes flour from his cuffs. A nurse waits for the first bus, watching her breath gather and vanish. Somewhere, a street sweeper nudges last night toward the gutter, while gulls argue over a paper bag.

I like this hour because nothing has decided what to become. Windows are still dark enough to hold reflections, and every café chair turned upside down looks briefly like a piece of sculpture. Even the pigeons seem uncertain, pacing the pavement as if searching for an appointment they forgot to write down.

Once, during such a morning, I found a piano standing beside a dumpster. Its varnish was scarred, and one yellowed key made no sound. I pressed another. A single note crossed the alley, startling a cat and waking an entire invisible geography of echoes. For a moment, I imagined carrying the piano home, though I lived three flights up and could barely play.

Instead, I left a coin on its lid, an absurd payment to whoever had abandoned music there. Weeks later, passing again, I saw only wet cardboard and a clean rectangle on the concrete.

Still, whenever dawn makes the streets feel newly invented, I remember that note. It taught me how little an object needs to become a door: one trembling string, one listening alley, one person foolish enough to stop. Perhaps that is enough: to answer briefly, then continue walking, carrying the sound farther than the hands can.
